projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Andrew Radonich was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: This -- what I'm here giving you is this is the 50th anniversary that's in a memorial of the 29th Division heroes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you want to read that? You don't have to read that in there. I mean, I'll have a copy of it.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Why don't you -- I can get it. "I'm writing to you as a member of Post 72 for many years. I always save my 29th souvenir of the division I served in. I've read many articles of men who have served in different combat companies during the war years, and not much has been written of the artillery units of the 224th Field Artillery Battalion. The 50th year reunion was meant a lot to me, and I lived to tell the end of the war, the occupation. I'm sending you a clipping from a local newspaper, a picture of me I saved. My Eisenhower jacket as it is all these years. I wanted my family to save the jacket. I pinned all my medals for them to have in remembrance of me. I'm also sending a picture of my car. You will see the license plates issued to me Victory Day, June the 6th. There were eight survivors. I asked for the special plates which equals Victory Day, June the 6th, and I'm the eighth owner of these, of these plates. I'm hoping you will be able to have these published in the 29er. Also enclosed is an article from the newspaper. I would like to hear from you, and let me know when you receive this article. I read so much about the other units, but the 29th. And I myself feel that in the artillery we were neglected. At least I tried and wanted to represent my unit -- let me find my notes -- represent my unit and how I felt serving in the Army. I am very proud of what I did and you should recognize my outfit. The men under Andrew Radonich had -- at this time I was 74 when I wrote this. I was a sergeant in the st Army, 29th Corps, 29th Division, 224th Field Artillery and supplied the artillery and small arms at Omaha Beach. For Radonich, the battle began in the early afternoon. I was the first truck to go ashore and man the 50-caliber machine gun going up the draw ?), which was a road between two hills. I saw the large German gun ship, coastal guns, out of commission. As he moved up, about 30 German prisoners had surrendered and were being taken back towards the beach. We went about two miles inland and then and behind the hedgerows and dug in for protection. We moved a short distance. We were told to unload our trucks and the of the howitzer ammunition and small caliber and grenades, and we were to pick up a infantry, a company of infantrymen and drive down to the front line. There we met the lieutenant colonel, who asked me -- asked if we had passed any American tanks. We had not, so he removed our trucks off the road. The tanks were coming in to load the -- to lay the attack. And we went back to the hedgerows, where we had camouflaged our ammunition. We didn't realize how many of our men had been killed and wounded. That was my first battle, the day I never forgot. I tried to, and was scared and wondered if I'd ever get back home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your hometown was Mentor-on-the-Lake?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Not at this time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. What was your hometown when the war started?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: I was -- I was drafted from Meritstown (ph), Pennsylvania. That's between Uniontown and Brownsville. I was drafted for one year in the first cycle of the draftees when they had the draft opening up. Because our country was so poor we had nothing, and they had -- the depression was coming. And I was sent to Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were drafted in early 1941? Is that about right?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. And on December the 7th I was ready to be discharged. I had one year. I was going home when two officers and two MPs came with my folder. He said, You're not going home." He said, "We're taking your discharge papers away, and you're going to be transferred to the 29th Division. You'll have a hard training for a year, and you're going to meet men that never knew nothing." They had men there that were National Guard because you had no place to live or feed. They joined the National Guard. That's where they were stationed. When I came there, I was a professional soldier. I was trained by a regular West Point captain. And I came there. A colonel come out and he looked at me. I was just only a private. One, two, or three, or four. But anyway, he says, "Well, Sergeant, you have a big job on your hand. We know nothing. The men you're going to see, you're going to be discouraged." And I walked in the barracks. I seen men with pajamas, all civilian clothes. They had fatigues on. That's all. I have a -- I was a professional soldier. I was dressed. My fatigues were starched and pressed. And I -- and they looked at me as if they'd never seen a real soldier. And so I went and got my supply . Supply sergeant issued all my stuff that I needed for my bunk, and I asked him for a rifle. He says, "I got them in a box. I don't know what to do with them. You do what you think you should." I took one rifle, an old 30-30 Springfield rifle, bolt action. All in . And I see these guys had them rifles. They were still up against the bed. And I asked, "Don't you guys know what to do?" They says, "We don't know nothing." I had to take -- I took them down where we washed the clothes and showered, and I took the rifles apart with hot water and GI soap, and I scrubbed it up and then I oiled it up and tightened up the strap, and I -- I was taught some of the fancy things with this captain from West Point how to kick the rifle and flip it up and bring it back down and bring it to attention. I did different things to show them, and they said, "Well, what does that all mean to me?" I said, "Well, you will learn." That was my start of my career in the 29th division. And we spent one year in the states. In 1942 -- I'd have to get my discharge paper, but I think it was getting fall when we left on the Queen Elizabeth in New York on Pier 90. First American troops to go overseas to England. We didn't know where we were going. We went without an escort. She traveled -- they said she could go up to 60 knots. There would be 10,000 men on one that there was eight floors high. Had elevators. Maybe 8000 men on the rail, and they'd hit that thing and return every six minutes. No German submarine could keep up with her. We had no escort. We traveled alone. And everybody bomb us, it went right down the line because everybody was seasick. And as we got -- we landed into Greenock, Scotland. We landed in the bay. They have -- they don't have water deep enough to take a big ship in. And where I landed in Greenock, Scotland was the first time they had these boats taking the soldiers off underground, and they're put so far, gone so far, and they drop you off. Then they had women there. You got a cup of tea and some crackers and a can of sardines, and when we got there. Now, before we went underground, I was looking around, and I see these lights that they have, spotted these German planes, maybe 30,000 feet up. They looked like little toys up there. And I happened -- and I walked over to the side, and I see they're firing antiaircraft guns. To my surprise, I see one woman. She's firing four of these guns because their men are fighting in the war. They manned the guns on the coastlines and in the cities because the men had to go into battle. They did the fighting for this country. And that was the first time I saw the first German planes, and the women operated the AAC-AAC guns. Then from there we went to a little town called Bloxun ph) in England. And I think that's in Oxford County. It's about 80 miles from London. And we came there. They unloaded us, and the people greeted us. They had nothing there, and they had the truck there, the two trucks. They were British soldiers, and they says, The church, and they had three high. They gave you a bag, and they had straw. You used that and filled up the straw, whatever you -- who wanted the top and bottom, that's where we slept, inside of this church, and we listened to their masses in their church. We stayed and then we started to move around in different parts of England. I went into Tidworth Barracks. We were there. We went to -- we camped where we had to go under live ammunition. They had all these big generals and everybody there. It's the first time that this has been done. They had mines that wouldn't hurt you, and they had barbed wire, and they had 30, -caliber, 105 and 75, all live ammunition shooting at dummy tanks. And we crawled underneath and going under barbed wire. And you got so far and then the targets came up and you fired your six rounds. And that's the first time I was under live ammunition. Knowing what I was going to go through when we go into war. And we trained. In England we lot of time, many times going to put the camouflage, some kind of a thing to -- so the car or truck could go underwater and wouldn't stall out. And then we prepared to go to the landing, and we didn't know where we were going. But we went to Plymouth, England is where all the 29th gathered. And we went into this big dormitory. They take a whole company at a time, and you sit there. An officer came out and talked to you, and he explained to you what you're going to encounter when you landed at the beach in Normandy. There they had the thing so with the sand, what kind of sand it was, what kind of trees that grow there, what kind of shrubs, what obstacles you have, where the mine fields were. It looked like somebody telling you you're going downtown shopping in the mall. You're going to walk to shore and there's going to be -- nothing's going to be worried about. But when -- when it came time, they stopped -- after we landed, they stopped forces from landing because the men wouldn't move because so many was -- so many men dead laying there, they had to clean the beaches up so the men would go forward and they could bring in more troops. But before this was all taking place, I seen a ship. It carried one whole regiment, and I could see when -- probably about ten miles from me, maybe closer, the big kind of battleship. Not battleship, but big gun emplacement that the Germans fired. It hit the front of that, made a great big hole. You could drive a truck through it when it hit the front, and they drove that all the way up onto the sand, and the men didn't get their feet wet. Now, I don't know if it was the 1st Division or the 4th Division or the 29th Division because we all had -- everybody had their own spot and place where they were going to land. And you -- and this sounds great. We were going to go to shore, no problem. But when they realized after we went -- and I had talked to you and told you about my experience in first time in battle. Not knowing until after what did we get ourselves into. But so many men. And we had lost 9263 men on the beach. And Eisenhower was 30 miles out in the channel on the battleship either Augusta or Texas. Because when they lifted up the gunfire, the Germans came from underground and were picking us off like flies. And that's when I told the men, "We're not going to stay here. Move away. I don't want nobody 30 feet from nobody. Close -- that's as close as you can be." We was going to stay there until we find out what's our next move. And that's when they asked me to take the trucks and unload everything that we had and go up, go here. And I had this map, which was just like a scribbly line. I have it somewhere. I saved it. And we were to pick up a company of infantry because they had lost so many men and 115th and 116th. So that was the first time that the 175th was held in reserve when -- to move up to go into combat. And that's when the colonel come out, "Sergeant, how in the hell did you get this far and you didn't have a tank? Didn't they tell you you got to -- you're supposed to get four tanks to come give you support?" I said, "Well, we had four machine guns." He said . He said, "That's a help." But he says, "You should have had your tanks. You should have never moved without them. You have the authority and nobody -- I myself can't tell you what to do. It's your job. You know what you have to do." And that's what the -- the army's -- you're in charge. If you're a platoon leader, your men don't do nothing unless you say so, even the squad leader, the sergeant can't tell him. He waits for me to say when you move. And as we moved into combat, went all the way into Saint-Lo, and it was -- I remember riding across the field and the two men who were infantry, and they were dropped. And we went in and it was dry and hot. And the dust was coming up, and the Germans, they had the th in Saint-Lo. They picked up them dust storms (?) and they laid the groundwork for artillery shell. Now, that 88th could either be for artillery, for tanks, or aircraft. It was one of the finest decent machine you ever saw compared to what we had. And I thought our army was the best equipped army that you had. But going back to the beach, to talk a little more about it, I have it in the book. You can look at it. We met the toughest division that the Germans had. They fought in Africa under Rommel. 352nd Infantry Division. And we were the first division ever in combat, and they were in combat fighting. Montgomery was fighting Rommel in the desert. Those men were well-heeled and they were -- they were real good soldiers. They were the best. I say they were better than we were because they had combat training, and they said that we were the best soldiers that they ever met, that they fought and kept together. They didn't panic and run. And I remember that, and I never forgot that the 352nd Infantry. I could show you on the map exactly where they were located and we hit the main head of it. And then we broke through to Saint-Lo, and then we went in to Avranches into France, and from there we were squeezed out with a V, spearheaded, and then we squeezed out and then we went for a rest. And then we went to Brest. That's up far -- so far up as you could go, and they had big coastal guns, and that was the -- Brest was the submarine pen for the Germans. And they had all kinds of sailors, soldiers, everything there that you could think of. And I could -- we were at -- I see maybe about two miles out, maybe three, Battleship Texas was out there firing, and we'd watch her sideways and move. And we took Brest and took a lot of prisoners. And from there we said we'd -- moving out, and we moved to take over another spot, and we were the first Americans in to Paris. And when we went into Paris, I -- the Eiffel Tower was I says, "Well, we're too far ahead. Let's just sit and wait." So we waited three days and four nights. Finally, troops came there, and I don't know who they were, but anyway, they were 29th. One officer said, How did you get this far, you men and y'all lived?" he says. But nobody went up. We stayed there. I said, Drop me down and I'll take a machine gun and I'll look on the other side to see what's on the other side. It's not that wide of a bridge." I went over. I says, Nothing there." So I says, "We're okay. But nobody moves." Do you think that we see any French people come out? Not one. I saw one old woman come out. She came out. She was begging for food. She had nothing to eat. We only had -- maybe we had one day's rations. But one of the men when we were going through the countryside, picked up rabbits at a farmhouse, and he gave her one rabbit. She thanked him. That was the only French woman that I saw. And after we went so far, we found out that the 24th Infantry Division just landed. They were spic and span because the 29th was ragged. They went and marched in Paris, but we were -- th is the one that took Paris. But we were ragged, and the men had to go through that. They didn't want to see us, how bad we looked. And I -- from my experience, I says, "They get such a big welcome. The people came from everywhere." I says, "Here we there all these days and never saw no Frenchmen." And so that -- and I tell my wife -- remember when Princess Diana was killed in that -- by that -- where the bridge is, where the Eiffel Tower is? I says, "Hon, I was right at that spot, right behind that tower there." And I remember that. Then we moved out of there into France. Then we went to Belgium, Holland -- no. Luxembourg. Belgium and Luxembourg, then Holland. We went out of Heerlen, and we were close to a little town named Kerkrade. And we stayed there for three weeks. And finally we moved out to go -- it was on the German border of Holland and Germany. And the first thing that we came to was the Siegfried line. I remember the Siegfried line with all the -- they have all of these things. They placed the mines and everything, big trenches so if they had tanks they would go down in and can't get out. And we went to the -- through this one part. And the town, the first town that we was taking was Aachen. That was the -- that was the largest town on the borderline because that was -- that was a coal mining part of Germany and Holland. And then from Aachen, then we traveled on to more parts of Germany until we came to the Ruhr River. On December the 25th, we sat at the Ruhr River. We couldn't cross over, and we dug in. No fires. Germans on the other hill; we're on this hill. And the people came out. They were German people. Gave us sheets to protect ourselves. We walked out in the snow because they couldn't pick you off because you're pretty far away. So they would -- then you couldn't have fires. And then finally the Bulge broke open on December the 25th. And the colonel come, says, "Sergeant, not you but every other man." I never saw him after that. After -- after they cleared up the Bulge, then we moved across the river. We moved so fast and taken a lot of towns. If they had pockets of soldiers only left just a handful of men to keep them contained until other units would follow up and take over and get them. And I went all the way to Germany to Bremerhaven. We're the first ones to enter Bremerhaven. Bremerhaven, Germany was all the people in the European countries along the Mediterranean or Italy, all of them countries, came to United States. They sailed from Bremerhaven. And I remember I was eight years old, ten years old, talking with my mother, and she was telling me that she was 18 and he was 20. They got married and they came to this country. And they came from Yugoslavia. She said that they crossed the Adriatic Sea to come to Italy. Then they took the -- the warship on the Mediterranean as far north as they could go, and they had to take a train to Bremerhaven, Germany, and she described the place to me. So many trains come in. This is like a big glass dome. It's so -- and ships are in there waiting to take people out. It was a very large place. And that's where they had a base where the fighter pilots would take off. And when we came there, and I -- I remembered my mother telling me about this when I was a little boy. Look at -- look at Andy. He's walking out there. He took everything off. Look at the Germans out there. Look at them. They're waving to him with white flags. And he just walked out. The colonel says, "Sergeant" -- he says, "Damn you." I said, "No, it's okay." I motioned for them to come out. I never saw so many surrender, and that's when they took the prisoners and we stayed there and they took the German occupation. There was many other incidents that happened, but I -- right now I can't think of anything. But I received a lot of medals. I'm proud of it. I came home. I went to Le Havre, France coming home on the point system. The highest point men got to come home first. But before we were sent home, I was transferred to the Fighting th. Not knowing we still had -- still had the war going on. Not knowing that when I went to the 69th it just took about six -- some of the other guys went there because they would be -- had going -- they going to be transferred to go to the Pacific. Me, I says fine. So I came there, and the captain says, "What would you like to have to eat, Sergeant? Steak? Pork chops? Chicken? You name it, we can feed you." Not knowing what was going to happen. And I have a book, and this is the book that I got, I got from there. And this shows you that I did not meet the Russians there, but they went into battle at Leipzig. Leipzig, Germany. That was their biggest battle that they had, and that was the only battle. And this book that I have here, my friend, I'm going to show it to him. He can see the picture of the Russian soldiers and the American soldiers that met at the Elbe River. See, we already went to the Elbe River. They wouldn't -- didn't let us go over to go. We were only about 60, 70 miles from Berlin. We waited for two and a half months for the Russians to take Berlin because we would have lost a million men. And I says -- and what my job was, we took turns. They says any way that they could cross the river. They had these trucks. They hold 250 men standing. They had them lined up, and you did the -- you did the counting how many you counted the shift that you worked, how many prisoners they were taking. That's also into my 29th Division book that I have here. All the men that were killed during World War II, all the men that are missing. In the book here -- you seen the movie Private Ryan, his name is listed in the book.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job specifically? Were you platoon leader?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I was a staff sergeant.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Staff sergeant, platoon leader?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were in charge of how many men?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: There was four squads, three or four squads.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So about 50 men almost?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: At full strength?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. Full strength. Yeah. Yeah. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of crossing the channel on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: We went to England. At Plymouth, England we crossed the channel. On the one I was on, every boat, every ship, no matter what was on the craft, had a cable 200 feet high. On each cable was a blimp, helium to fill it in case the planes came over to strafe the ship going into the beach, going to cross the channel. They would have to cut -- they fly low enough they'll hit them and they'll crash. Otherwise they could wipe you out. And then it got bad, the weather got bad for two days. That's when they said that they were calling it off because men were sick. The water was -- the waves were so big. You looked up, that big wave was coming at you. That was a terrible day. And then it quieted down. I understand that -- and we landed at Omaha Beach -- that Eisenhower told Bradley that we're pulling back. We lost too many men. We can't go forward. The 4th and the 1st Division had no casualties. 29th suffered the most casualties during World War II all through the battle. If anybody wants to see my book, I have a list of all the men that were killed, all the units that were -- served with the 29th and men that died. I saw many men. And I have everything that I showed with this conversation we're having here, all my medals. I have papers to prove I had them medals. I couldn't get them if I -- without that. So then I want to show you a picture of my mother and father when they came to this country. They were two young people. I will be right back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Pennsylvania. That's where I grew up at. We lived in Cleveland and my mom couldn't stand the smell because it's a steel mill. I lived between 55th and Broadway. And she was always sick. She was a young lady. She said that was not for her. And he had -- she had -- he had a brother that lived in Pennsylvania working the mines, and her father worked on the railroad. And we -- we went to move to this one town called Geneva, Pennsylvania, and he had a job where they made glass (?). It was too hot. He said he didn't like it, so he got somehow contacted with his -- her father and his brother to come to this little town called Briar Hill (ph), Pennsylvania, and I remembered I was maybe five years old. I didn't go to school yet. But we had three teams of horses, all the chickens, pigs, cows, and oxen. My mother knew how to drive oxen, and we moved to Pennsylvania and then we had -- then we moved and farmed there. And that's where I grew up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of buddies over there? Overseas?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Only one that I write to, he's in Salem, West Virginia, Johnnie Helms. He always hung by himself. He was like a quiet type of a person. He wasn't radical. He didn't do things like other people do, and he kind of took a liking to me. So we stuck together all the time and we still write together. Every Christmas we write cards and send pictures. And I'll be 83 this November, and my wife's just turned 80. We're married 56 years, and I have a son that was in Vietnam. He was wounded. He spent two months at the veterans hospital here in Cleveland. And I have a daughter and six grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything with that buddy when you were overseas? Doing anything --

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Together, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- together?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Just -- just he was always looked for me because he was always afraid. Because I -- he says, "You were too calm. You were quiet, and you were the type of a person that I never saw before." When you see -- he says, "These guys if a guy did something the sergeant would scream and yell in his face. You never did that. You were a man, but you were young. You were strong and powerful, and nobody could do anything with you. You had your mind." And he says, "You were trusted. Every man trusted you. They'd protect you no matter what." And you wanted to see that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, you know, what else I wanted to ask you. When you said when you first got over there to England you were underground. Do you mean that you were literally underground or what were you talking about?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: No. When we went to Scotland, landed in Scotland, oh, yes. We were underground.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They kept you underground just so that the Germans would have no idea you were there?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Right. They didn't see you. Because they had these search lights. They had -- they had these four planes up there. There was like three search lights or four on each one had the plane. That's where the AAC AAC guns were, the AAC AAC firing gun. When that -- well, getting back to England, we were stationed on the channel side of England, and they had the buzz bombs. Now, their buzz bombs are flown -- they have no motors or no personnel. They keep about 2000 feet above the water, and they'd go in as far as they can, and that's what they were hitting, the big cities in England like London. They were ten-ton buzz bombs that would explode. They put the fires in, that's all. People there in London -- and I was in London several times -- they lived all underground because they were always under attack by the Germans. And I could remember -- I have it in the book. I'd have to look it up -- I see this we weren't involved in it, but I seen this one sergeant. I says, "What have you got there?" He says, "That's where they launched the first rockets that was ever made." And he said, "Good thing you're here, Sergeant. did not kill no scientists. All the civilians that built that rocket." I have the picture in the book that was taken that showed the launching pad when they fired the rockets.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: In Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Germany?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. Or was it in France? I'd have to look.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Czechoslovakia?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: No. In France.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. That's where it was. In France they launched them into England.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: And they -- I say today without those German scientists, we wouldn't be that far ahead in the rocket ships because they were way ahead of us. And I've said -- and they crossed the Elbe River. See something coming out of the sky. That's the first time I saw a Andrew Radonich October 26, 2001 jet plane. Mind you, that's in 1944 in December when I saw first jet plane. Came down and dropped its two bombs and left. That's all I ever saw. That's a picture. I have that picture where this happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that the Messerschmitt-262?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: What was it? Me-109.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Or Me-262, I think.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: That's the -- they have the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The 109 was the regular fighter.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Fighter.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Now, they had the Spitfire that the English had was compared with their little fighter they had.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Now our Thunderbolt, our P-47, they had that plane because compared to that the only way you could tell the two is by the propeller that points.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Ours is straight. Theirs is offset.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: When we were -- when we had crossed through the Siegfried line, we went into Auzorp (ph) on New Years Day. It was -- the sun came out. It was snowing out and it was melting, and the Germans' planes came over -- came out. That's the first time 10, 12, 15 planes. Be watching them come over. We're not firing, but the antiaircrafts were stationed all over, were firing at them. And I looked -- I seen this plane coming, so I ran into a bunker and then come back out. And it exploded, and I seen this pilot come down, and he landed. And it was an officer, a German fighter pilot. And he landed his parachute. And I ran up to him. I didn't touch him. I didn't take nothing from him. I didn't look for nothing. And I seen he was bleeding. He had that white thing, and I put it under his arm. I lit up a cigarette and put it in his mouth, and I went back. I asked the guy that speaks German, he says, "Is he saying anything to you, Andy?" And he says yeah. I says he says to me Danka. I said, "What did he mean by that?" He said, "Oh, he thanked you for not executing him." That's one of the experiences. But you were asking me about that medal that I got. Oh, this is a picture that I made of my medals.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, that's good. Do you remember getting letters from home, getting mail and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Did I ever get any letters?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Do you remember anything about letters? Packages?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: I got -- my wife that I'm married to -- she's in the bedroom -- she sent me packages. In fact, we were in -- I forget the German town. It was at Christmastime. She sent me a big package of cookies, all crushed up, and she sent me a tie clasp and some other jewelry that she sent me at Christmastime because she didn't know what to send me, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything in particular for entertainment or to relieve the tension when you were over there?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: No. I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No time for that?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: No. I had no kind of -- we would go to a rest area and they take you there and they gave you meals, and they had the band play music and they'd bring women from these towns that come to their dances. That's about all that I think for entertainment. And then when we were in Salzwedel, and there was -- we hadn't had a shower in three months. So the engineers rigged up in the hills, and they had fire, and these water lines going through the fire and they told us, okay, now -- and a quartermaster was there to give you clean clothes because you looked too -- all worn out and raggedy, you know, and they had people there that knew how to sew all this stuff on. And you went to -- and you had a line, and everybody was taking a shower. First time in three or four months. And it was cold, but it was a good shower. I'm going to show you -- I saved this. This is -- we're going back to the civilian life in 1937 during depression. This was a man's pay stub. And when you work in the mines and his total for that he worked for was $56.27, and he owed the company $8.41. Now, his smithy checkup -- check -- check money he paid 43 cents. Union dues was 65 cents. Assessment was 25 cents. You used dynamite, was $1.75. Lamp and oil was 42 cents. Smithing was 23 cents. Rent, $3.75 a month. The doctor for the month was 68 cents. And you want to review that? You ever saw one like that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was amazing. Do you have any specific memories about your homecoming, when you first saw your family when you got back?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: When I came home -- I was discharged from Indiantown Gap. They were outside, and they + on your jacket, and you were free to go. And we are standing in line, and I asked the guys, "What are you guys waiting for?" He says, "Well, we don't know how. They don't have nothing here to send you home." You can't hitchhike because no cars. You're Indiantown Gap. I see a guy walking, and I says to him, I says, "Hey." I said, "Do you know we're all going to Pittsburgh, right?" I said, "Everybody's going to Pittsburgh." How many guys? Oh, it was about 60, 70, 80 men. I says, well, I'm going to take somebody with me. I say, each one of you guys give me five bucks. We're going to go -- I'm going to go into Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and get a -- see if we can get Greyhound buses to take us to Pittsburgh. Went there and got two buses and we came back with the buses, and the guys all loaded up and told them how much it was. He wouldn't take the money, and they asked if we go to a town, stop and they got some liquor. Some of the guys had +. We got into Pittsburgh and got out. I don't know my way around in Pittsburgh, so I was walking up the street and a man and woman pulled over to the side. Says, Did you just get off that Greyhound bus?" I says, yeah. I says, "How do I get to Uniontown?" He says, "First we want to take you out." so we went in there and gave me a meal and he says, "There's a Greyhound bus that goes to Uniontown." And I went to Uniontown and got off the bus. I knew where I was at. So I knew I get off and I walked up to the Route , and I hitchhiked home from there. There was a little town of Briar Hill, and there it was on top of that hill. They had a beer joint. I stopped in there, but I didn't know anybody in there. I knew the man that owned it, and he offered me anything I wanted to drink. I says no. And I says, "I just want to go home." And everybody was looking at me, and I says, "I want to walk home. I used to walk here, I can walk that far." It was about two miles from there. And the guy says, "No. Somebody's going to take you home." Okay. So he dropped me off at the bottom of the hill, and I went up the hill and I hollered. Mom let the dog out, jumped at me. And I walked into the kitchen. My mother and father didn't know that I was coming home, and they just sat there, unbelieving -- after three years they haven't seen me -- that I'm alive. And that's when I started my civilian life. [END OF SIDE A OF TAPE. BEGINNING SIDE B OF TAPE.]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What do you think of -- going back to D-Day and backtracking a bit, when you think of D-Day, does one vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Well, yes. The first time when I saw these rangers were on horses, and they got orders not to take prisoners. And I was on a 50-caliber machine gun, and they said, "We're not going any farther." I turned my gun down. I refused. I said, "They're yours. That's your responsibility. My men behind me is my responsibility. I want no part of them. You take them to the beach. I remember that part, you know. And I -- the officer we had, I very seldom saw him. Maybe -- I don't remember seeing Captain Merson (ph) maybe once or twice, maybe not even at all. I had guys that took battlefield commissions, the lieutenants. Everyone that took a battlefield commission two weeks, three weeks at the most, he was dead. I have it in the book here. I'll show it to you, that they're listed right there. I knew the guy real personally. They were good sergeants, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's go. 29, let's go was your motto, huh?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. When we started off at the this is the thing that I had here, Andrew Radonich was born November the 30th, 1919 in Cleveland, Ohio. Was drafted on second cycle for the Meritstown (ph), Pennsylvania, 1941. Inducted to Fort Bragg, North Carolina. Completed basic training, was assigned to the 29th Infantry Division, 110 Field Artillery, later be 224th. And it goes on to tell you during the war years, peacetime in the Army, he earned a medal for good conduct, American Events Service Medal, European-African Middle East medal with four bronze battle stars, one bronze arrow on D-Day, one occupation of Germany, the Bronze Star for meritorious service, chief ammunition section, 224th Field Artillery. In to March 1945, military operations against the enemy with western Europe, SS 03 rifle sharpshooter. Sharpshooter for carbine and belongs to Limestone Post in Baltimore, Maryland. That's just a little history thing that they had on me, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Well, I tried to present myself as best as I know how. And in order to -- I talked with fellows and they say, "Oh, you never say nothing. Was you -- did you ever hear about this?" "Oh, yeah. I was there." See, it bothered me for a long time. I was really depressed. I went to -- you know, had to go to treatment because it was too much about this service stuff. So now I got kind of away from it and don't let it bother me that much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: This is the first time --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: -- I ever discussed my life with somebody and things that happened, you know. Because I know if I talk to guys and sometimes I look at them, I don't say nothing, but sometimes I say to myself, Man, he sure is exaggerating. Because it's only two -- there's only one way you can do. Tell the truth, you know. Oh, I was in the Army in World War II. Oh, yeah. I says, "I was with the 29th Infantry Division." I says, "I landed Omaha Beach on D-Day," you know. But I don't talk too much about it anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, did you have some trouble adjusting when you got back in the --

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah. Q -- first couple of years?

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Oh, yeah. First -- first three or four years. My wife would be scared to sleep. She'd -- boy, she says, You get up in that bed, you was really yelling out." It took a while, she says, but then she got over it, you know. But then when we -- they had stuff that we'd + and they'll show something and she'll call me. She says, "Did you ever hear of that town?" I says, "Yeah, I was there," you know. And in fact I talked to a couple. They went to Paris and they said they'd go on their own. So they decided to go -- I didn't mention it -- on their own. They went to where they fought the first world war. Outside of Paris when we -- when they went we were going towards, I think it was Belgium or Luxembourg, and we -- they stopped, and I went -- we were going to the cemetery. They're all marble crosses. World War I soldiers that were gassed that were buried there. Thousands upon thousands. I went and looked at names of all of them. I found one man from the 29th Division when that -- at that time. And I met a woman, and she had a brother. He was buried in Holland in a big cemetery there. Most of the ones during the D-Day, lot of them were buried right there at the beach. I don't think -- I never heard of anybody sending bodies back. You know, they had them buried right there. And I forgot to tell you. When I was in the service I was getting $21 a month. Was big pay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: We was a poor country. We went -- when that depression came and then they started -- Roosevelt became president. Hoover was the one put a chicken in every pot and a car in every driveway. And we went to depression. We were so poor this country couldn't even feed their own people. I could remember when the trucks came to the coal mine. They had like old soleside (ph), potatoes, flour, different things that they distributed food for the people because that's the only way the government could feed them. But see, over there, the people had gardens. They knew how to survive. They had chickens, pigs, and cows. They could survive it. But the people in the cities, they lived off the dumps or whatever they threw away. That's where they went to pick up their food, you know. It was a -- they say the good old days, but you always have to remember people that came to this country were foreign people from all over the world came here. They all had big families. They all had good sons. They never -- only thing they had was cigarettes, chew tobacco, and beer and moonshine. We never heard of drugs and things like that. And they were all good young men. And when they fought World War II they saved the world. Yet 292,000 men that died during World War II, they gave up their life for you people to live a better life than what we had. And they saved the world. And just today I always say this: My generation will be the greatest generation in the world. There will never be another generation like it. Believe me. And you know that. Probably your father to you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. My dad was pretty humble about it, but I certainly realize that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Andrew Radonich
sp.p: Yeah.
